title: Texas’s Audit-Enforcement List Expanded. Hallsville Is Named.
thumbnailMessage: Hallsville is named. Current status still needs records.
summary: An August 17 state record names Hallsville among more than 110 additional cities sent audit-compliance determination letters. Current compliance and the applicable tax-year consequence still need city-specific records.
content:
## Correction and update — October 3, 2026

Texas’s municipal audit-enforcement list grew after RepWatchr’s August 8 report. An August 17 announcement from the attorney general’s office says violation-determination letters went to more than 110 additional cities. Hallsville appears by name in that original state record.

That establishes a historical state action. It does not establish Hallsville’s current compliance status, whether a later filing resolved the issue, or whether any tax rate the city adopted was unlawful. Those answers require city-specific records that this desk has not obtained.

## What the later list adds

The attorney general’s August announcement follows its earlier action involving more than 130 cities. Its additional list also includes Hawkins, Hudson, Linden, New London, Overton and Winnsboro. The office describes an investigation of municipal audit and financial-statement requirements under Senate Bill 1851.

An audit-compliance determination is not a finding of stolen money or corruption. The distinction matters: a resident should be able to ask for the financial records without treating a missing or late filing as proof of a different offense.

## The tax year needs a correction

Our August report broadly framed the May enforcement list as a restriction on the 2026 tax-rate season. That was too categorical without examining each city’s determination date and the law’s tax-year language.

The enrolled SB 1851 text links the no-new-revenue restriction to a tax year beginning on or after the attorney general’s determination, and to qualifying later tax years before the required audit or filing is completed. The effective date was September 1, 2025. A city’s fiscal year, a tax year and the date a council votes on a rate are separate parts of that analysis.

In its August 21 update, the Texas Municipal League interprets a determination issued during calendar 2026 as applying to tax year 2027 rather than automatically limiting the rate adopted during 2026. TML advises cities to confirm that interpretation with their city attorney and financial advisers. That is TML’s stated interpretation; this report has not obtained an individual determination letter or a ruling settling its application to Hallsville.

We therefore do not describe every city on either historical list as currently prohibited from adopting a particular rate. Nor does a city’s appearance on the list settle the legality of an already adopted tax rate.

## The records needed next

For Hallsville and other named cities, the useful packet is specific: the determination letter and date, the audited financial statement and auditor’s opinion, the clerk’s filing receipt, any state correspondence about compliance, and the adopted tax-rate order and calculation worksheet.

Those records would allow a dated comparison between what the state determined and what the city subsequently completed. Until then, current compliance and the applicable tax-year consequence remain open questions. A press release from either side cannot replace that record.

This update preserves the original August 8 publication date. The August 17 enforcement expansion is a newly incorporated historical source, not an enforcement action announced today.
